subtype: Catching the mood of a parent [Receiver]
passage: Rain drummed on the car roof, and the traffic to Masi's wedding reception hadn't moved for twenty minutes. Abhinav's mother, Kavitha, said nothing. She just gripped the steering wheel and kept looking at the clock. In the back, Abhinav, five, stopped driving his toy bus. He watched her shoulders. Then he began to whimper. "I want to sit with you." "Not now, Abhi." Big tears came. "I don't want to go." Kavitha saw his wet face in the mirror. She breathed out slowly, reached back and squeezed his foot. "Amma's worried about being late. Not about you."

qa.q: How long had the traffic not moved?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav start to whimper, though nobody had scolded him?
qa.a: He picked up his mother's tension from her tight grip and silence, and her worry became his own.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that could help Abhinav feel safe again?
qa.a: She breathed out slowly, squeezed his foot and told him she was worried about being late, not about him.

qa.q: How might the drive have felt to Kavitha once she saw Abhinav's wet face?
qa.a: She was already stressed about being late, and his tears likely showed her that her mood had spread to him, so she softened.

grounding: A young child in a stuck car senses his mother's silent tension before a family event and becomes clingy and tearful, though nothing was said to him.

subtype: Catching the mood of a parent [Receiver]
passage: In their Chennai flat, the relatives were coming at six for Paati's sixtieth birthday, and Vandana rushed between the kitchen and the hall with her lips pressed tight. She didn't shout. She just moved fast and sighed over the payasam. Sahil, four, left his blocks and followed her, holding the end of her dupatta. When she went to the balcony, he went too. When she said, "Sahil, go and play," his chin wobbled and he burst into tears. Vandana stopped. She knelt and hugged him. "Amma's in a rush, kanna. You haven't done anything." Then she let him stir the payasam.

qa.q: What did Sahil hold as he followed Vandana around?
qa.a: The end of her dupatta.

qa.q: Why did Sahil burst into tears when he was told to go and play?
qa.a: He had soaked up his mother's rushed, tight mood, and being sent away made the worry spill over.

qa.q: What helped Sahil settle once Vandana noticed?
qa.a: She knelt, hugged him, said he hadn't done anything and let him stir the payasam, bringing him close instead of sending him off.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt when she saw Sahil crying?
qa.a: She probably felt a pang on seeing that her silent stress had passed to him, which is why she stopped and knelt down.

grounding: A small child picks up his mother's unspoken tension before relatives arrive and becomes clingy and tearful.

subtype: Laughter and panic in a class [Actor]
passage: In the silent reading period at their Delhi school, the only sound was the ceiling fan. Then Ojas's stomach growled, long and low, like a creaky door. Sumit snorted. He clapped a hand over his mouth, but his shoulders shook. That set off the girl behind him, then the whole back row. Soon the class was wheezing, heads down on their books, and nobody even remembered why. Sumit's eyes streamed. Every time he tried to stop, he looked at Ojas, and it started again. Ma'am waited, then said, "Two minutes to laugh. Then books." They laughed harder, and then, slowly, it ran out.

qa.q: What sound set everything off?
qa.a: Ojas's stomach growled, long and low.

qa.q: Why couldn't Sumit stop laughing, even when he wanted to?
qa.a: He felt giddy and helpless to stop, as the laughter all around kept feeding his own and every look at Ojas started it again.

qa.q: Why did Ma'am's "two minutes to laugh" work better than scolding might have?
qa.a: It let the giggles run their course instead of fighting them, so they faded on their own and the class could go back to books 🙂

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt as the whole class laughed?
qa.a: Ojas may have felt embarrassed at first, but since nobody even remembered why they were laughing, it likely became shared fun rather than mockery.

grounding: A growling stomach sets off one snort that spreads through the whole class until nobody remembers why they are laughing.

subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
passage: Sonali had come to the Kolkata football derby only because Darshan had a spare ticket. She didn't know a single player's name. But when sixty thousand people rose for the first attack, she rose too. By half-time she was shouting a chant she'd learnt ten minutes earlier, arms around strangers. When the referee waved off a goal, a roar of anger rolled down the stand, and Sonali found herself yelling at a man in black she could barely see, fists up, face hot. Darshan stared at her. "You?" In the ninety-first minute they scored, and she hugged an uncle she'd never met. On the metro home, voice gone, she felt oddly empty and oddly happy. "I don't even like football," she croaked. "Tonight you did," said Darshan.

qa.a: Darshan was astonished, since the Sonali he knew didn't even follow football, which is why he stared and said "You?"

subtype: Setting the tone of a team [Response]
passage:
Tuesday, late
Today I watched my own mood walk around the studio. At the ten o'clock stand-up I was already snapping: "Why isn't scene 12 rendered?" Jasleen went quiet. By lunch two animators were arguing over a shared file, and someone slammed a drawer. Nobody had yelled at them. I had just been sighing at everything for three days, and they'd caught it.
So at the four o'clock check-in I tried something. Before walking in, I stood by the water cooler and breathed out slowly, three times. Then I said, "Honestly, the client deadline scares me too. We're behind. Let's pick the three scenes that matter most." Jasleen actually laughed. The room loosened. We made a list.
Note to self: they read my face more than my slides.
Jatin

qa.q: What did Jatin do by the water cooler?
qa.a: Breathed out slowly, three times.

qa.q: What did Jatin realise about the tense mood by lunch?
qa.a: Jatin realised the team had caught three days of sighing and snapping, even though nobody had yelled at them.

qa.q: What changed at the four o'clock check-in, and why did it work?
qa.a: Jatin took a breath first, then admitted the deadline was scary and suggested picking three key scenes, which calmed the room and gave it a plan.

qa.q: What might the ten o'clock stand-up have been like for Jasleen?
qa.a: Jasleen went quiet under the snapping, probably feeling blamed and tense, which makes Jasleen's laugh at four o'clock a real sign of relief.

grounding: A young team lead notices their stress spreading through the studio, then takes a breath and speaks honestly about the pressure, and the team settles.

subtype: Being known as fair or a cheat [Actor]
passage: Behind the rice mill in the village, the boys played marbles in the dust every evening. Imran always paid what he owed. If he lost three, he dug three out of his pocket, even his favourite green one. Arnab was faster and cleverer, but twice last week he nudged his marble with his toe while the others were looking at the sky, and once he said, "I never said three, I said two." On Friday, when Imran arrived, four boys shouted, "Imran, our side!" When Arnab arrived, they went quiet and looked at their marbles. Nobody said "cheat". Nobody had to. Arnab stood at the edge, kicking a stone. By the time the mill siren went, nobody had asked him once.

qa.q: What did Imran do when he lost three marbles?
qa.a: He dug three out of his pocket, even his favourite green one.

qa.q: What might Arnab have been feeling as he kicked a stone at the edge?
qa.a: He likely felt left out and embarrassed, sensing the others no longer trusted him, even though nobody said "cheat".

qa.q: What could Arnab do to start earning back a place in the game?
qa.a: He could own up to the toe-nudges, pay what he owes, and play straight for many evenings, since trust will come back only slowly.

qa.q: How do the other boys see Imran and Arnab now?
qa.a: They see Imran as someone who keeps his word and want him on their side, while Arnab's clever play no longer counts because they can't trust him.

grounding: In a village marbles game, a boy who always pays up is welcomed while a boy who cheated a few times is quietly left out.

passage:
Thursday
Experiment update. Two weeks ago I told Dilnaz something small: that I can't ride a cycle, at fifteen. Not a huge secret. But if it got round, the boys in our class would never let it go.
I waited. Nothing. On Monday Rohit made cycle jokes about someone else, and Dilnaz just looked at me and said nothing. Not a wink, not a hint. Nothing!
So today in the library I told her the real one: about Papa losing his job, and why I've stopped going to the canteen. She listened, then asked if I wanted to share her tiffin, and didn't make it weird.
I know it's strange to test a friend. But last year Megha told the whole class about my braces photo within a day, and I still think about it. This time I went slowly. It worked.
Sharmila

qa.q: What small secret did Sharmila tell Dilnaz first?
qa.a: That Sharmila can't ride a cycle, at fifteen.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila want to test Dilnaz with a small secret first?
qa.a: Sharmila was still hurt by Megha spreading the braces photo last year, and wanted proof Dilnaz could keep something private before trusting more.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the library, and why did it feel safe?
qa.a: After two weeks of silence about the cycle, Sharmila shared the real worry about Papa's job; Dilnaz had already shown she could keep quiet, so the bigger step felt safe.

qa.a: Dilnaz might be a little surprised but could understand, given how Sharmila had been hurt before, and might feel glad to have earned the trust.

grounding: A teenager shares a small secret with a new friend to see if it stays private, and only then shares a bigger one, still remembering an old breach.

passage: In the placement cell's waiting room, Sachin heard his own sentence read aloud. "I first fell in love with bridges when..." It was from his cover letter. Now his face burned. He felt stupid more than angry. That night he sat on his bed, laptop open, deleting shared folders one by one. His roommate looked up. "Going to trust nobody now?" Chetan,
I'm writing because saying it out loud would come out as shouting.
In September you borrowed my camera for your cousin's wedding. "Back by Monday," you said. It's December. When I asked last week, you said it was "at home somewhere", and then I saw it in your photos from the beach trip.

passage:
Vice-principal's note, staff induction, week two.
Gopika, our new chemistry teacher, asked me today how everyone already seems to "know" each other. She told me what she has overheard in the staff room: "Karthik will always cover your period if you're ill." "Don't lend the lab key to Mr Rao, you'll never see it again." "Ask Beena, she answers emails the same day." Gopika has not worked with any of them yet, but she has already chosen Karthik for the joint science fair. I said such names are built from years of small, repeated things: returned keys, covered classes, quick replies. She was quiet, then said, "So they're already deciding what I am, too." I told her yes, and that the first month counts. I have paired her with Karthik for the fair and will review how it goes.

qa.q: Whom did Gopika choose for the joint science fair?
qa.a: Karthik.

passage: In their Hyderabad office, Himani's manager called her in about the job she was "apparently" applying for.
